title: Comet Halcyon-7
summary: A comet fragment will hit the Earth in nineteen months. The General Assembly must agree who leads the mission to deflect it, whether a nuclear blast is allowed, who pays to evacuate the Marelle Islands, and whether anyone may mine the comet.

committee.name: General Assembly: the approach of comet Halcyon-7 (practice)
committee.notes: Fictional scenario for practice: the comet, the Marelle Islands and every country's position are invented.

topic.name: The approach of comet Halcyon-7 (fictional scenario)
topic.notes: Fictional scenario. Every country position is invented and labelled Unverified demo.

tags.data_sharing: Requires States to share comet tracking data openly
tags.deflection: Sets up and funds a joint mission to deflect the fragment
tags.un_command: Puts the mission under UN coordination, not one State
tags.nuclear_option: Allows a nuclear device in space as a last resort
tags.relief_fund: Funds evacuation and relief for the impact zone
tags.liability: Holds launching States liable for damage from the mission
tags.no_claims: Bars any State or company from claiming the comet's resources

preambular.text: Alarmed that astronomers have confirmed that comet fragment Halcyon-7 is on course to strike the Earth in nineteen months,
Recalling that outer space is free for exploration and use by all States and is not subject to national appropriation,
Noting with concern that the most likely impact zone lies in the ocean beside the Marelle Islands, home to 400,000 people,
Recognising that only a few States have rockets able to reach the fragment in time,

operative.text: Calls upon every Member State with an observatory to share its tracking data on Halcyon-7 openly and in real time;
Decides to establish a joint mission to deflect the fragment, paid for by contributions from Member States in proportion to their means;
Requests that the mission be coordinated by the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs rather than by any single State;
Authorises the use of a nuclear device in space to deflect the fragment, but only if every other method has failed;
Establishes a relief fund to evacuate and shelter the people of the Marelle Islands until the danger has passed;
Affirms that the States launching the mission remain liable for any damage caused by its rockets or debris;
Declares that no State or company may claim ownership of the fragment or of any material taken from it.

news.headline: A second fragment is spotted behind Halcyon-7
news.body: Observatories report a smaller fragment trailing the first. It would probably fall into open ocean, but only three countries have shared the tracking data needed to be sure.

news.headline: A mining company says it will claim the comet
news.body: Starward Minerals says it will launch a probe within a year and keep whatever it brings back. Lawyers say States cannot claim the comet; whether a company can is less clear.

news.headline: The Marelle Islands ask the world for help
news.body: The islands' government says it can move only a third of its people on its own. It asks the General Assembly for ships, money and places for families to stay.

news.headline: The launch window is closing
news.body: Mission planners say a deflection rocket must leave within five months to have a good chance. Every month of delay makes it more likely the nuclear option will be needed.

cards.text: Urges every Member State with an observatory to share each new Halcyon-7 reading within seven days, and requests help for States that lack equipment;
Encourages Member States to share tracking data on Halcyon-7 voluntarily, and invites them to do so when they are able;
Requests the Secretary-General to appoint an independent panel of scientists to review every deflection plan before launch and to report to the Assembly;
Decides that a nuclear device may be used in space only with the further agreement of the Assembly and under inspection by international experts;
Calls upon Member States to keep nuclear devices out of the mission and to concentrate on non-nuclear methods of deflection;
Decides that contributions to the relief fund shall follow a sliding scale, with the poorest States exempt and launching States paying a larger share;
Invites private companies to contribute to the mission and to the relief fund, on condition that they make no claim to the fragment or its material;
Decides that scientific samples taken from the fragment shall be shared with all Member States for research and shall not be sold;

events.title: A small observatory publishes all its readings
events.body: An observatory in a small State posts every Halcyon-7 reading online and invites others to do the same. Delegates start asking who is still holding data back.
events.teaches: Open data lets others check your work, which is why shared evidence builds trust between States.

events.title: Marelle families wait on the quay
events.body: Reporters describe families on the Marelle Islands packing what they can carry and waiting for ships that have not been promised. Delegates feel pressure to say who will pay.
events.teaches: Humanitarian needs often move a debate faster than legal arguments, because delegates must answer to their own public.

events.title: Starward Minerals tests its probe
events.body: Starward Minerals announces a test flight of its probe. Lawyers in several capitals ask whether the company could keep what the probe collects.
events.teaches: Space law was written for States, so new private activity can open gaps that only new agreements can close.

events.title: The Pacific group meets in the corridor
events.body: Island delegations meet to compare notes on Halcyon-7. They are warm to any delegate who listens to their concerns rather than just their votes.
events.teaches: Regional groups often agree a shared line before a vote, so time spent listening to them can matter more than a speech.

events.title: The Marelle delegate asks to speak
events.body: The delegate of the Marelle Islands asks for the floor and describes plans for the evacuation in plain terms. Several delegates say afterwards that it changed how they saw the draft.
events.teaches: A State with little power can still gain influence by speaking clearly about what is at stake for its people.

events.title: Mission planners offer an early briefing
events.body: Engineers from the planning team offer to brief delegates before the next session. Those who attend can plan their time better.
events.teaches: Technical experts help diplomats understand what is possible, so agreements are built on facts rather than guesses.
